explanations.explanation: Silver, friend. Joseph tells his steward to put each man's silver in the mouth of his sack, along with all the food they can carry. Joseph is the ruler over Egypt, and this isn't the first time he has slipped silver back in their sacks (Genesis 42:25). He's making a habit of it.

Spices did make the trip to Egypt, because their father had them carry some as part of a gift for the ruler (Genesis 43:11). But that's not Joseph's order here. He tells the steward to put each man's silver back in the mouth of his sack. I'd have loved a spice rack in there, but the text says silver.

The brothers did bring a gift to Joseph and bowed down as they gave it (Genesis 43:26). So I see why gifts came to mind. But Joseph's order to the steward here is about silver, one man's silver in the mouth of each man's sack. The gifts had already been handed over.

That's the one. Joseph says, "Put my cup, the silver one, in the mouth of the youngest one's sack…" It goes in along with the silver for Benjamin's grain. Benjamin is the youngest brother, and he has no idea he's carrying a cup that belongs to the ruler of Egypt. Quietest delivery in the whole story.

Joseph did wear a signet ring, and Pharaoh, Egypt's king, was the one who gave it to him (Genesis 41:42). But the text never puts a ring in any sack. Joseph's order is for his cup, the silver one, in the youngest one's sack. The ring stays on his hand.

Pharaoh really did put a gold chain around Joseph's neck (Genesis 41:42). It's a fine piece of jewelry, but it never goes into a sack in this story. What Joseph has the steward put in the youngest one's sack is his silver cup. The chain stays right where Pharaoh put it.

explanations.answer: Why have you repaid good with evil
explanations.explanation: Right, and notice how big that question is. Joseph tells the steward to ask, "Why have you repaid good with evil?" It's a loaded line to throw at men who have no clue anything is missing. They've just been fed at Joseph's table, so I think it's meant to sting.

explanations.answer: Why did you leave before the dawn
explanations.explanation: Close on the timing, because they did head out at daybreak. But nobody is accused of leaving too early. The question Joseph hands his steward is, "Why have you repaid good with evil?" The brothers had left when they were sent, so the dawn isn't the problem.

explanations.answer: Why did you lie about your brother
explanations.explanation: Joseph's question has nothing about a brother, and nobody gets called a liar on this ride. The steward is told to ask, "Why have you repaid good with evil?" Then he adds the part about the cup. The brothers have no idea yet what they're being charged with.

I get why you'd think so, since the accusation sounds serious. But the brothers don't admit a thing. They answer, "Your servants could not possibly do such a thing." They're sure they're innocent, and they haven't seen what's in Benjamin's sack yet.

Right, they deny it flat out. They say, "Your servants could not possibly do such a thing." They have no idea the cup is in Benjamin's sack. Imagine being accused of stealing and having nothing to hide but a heavy feeling in your stomach.

explanations.answer: They brought back the silver they found
explanations.explanation: That's their argument. They say, "We even brought back to you from the land of Canaan the silver we found in the mouths of our sacks." Then they ask why they'd steal silver or gold from the house of the steward's master. They figure men who return money they could have kept aren't cup thieves.

explanations.answer: They never once left the steward's sight
explanations.explanation: The brothers never say anything like that. Their case rests on the silver they found in their sacks and brought back from Canaan. They ask, "Why would we steal silver or gold from your master's house?" Honest men don't need an alibi when they've got a receipt like that.

explanations.answer: They swore an oath before Pharaoh himself
explanations.explanation: No oath before Pharaoh, Egypt's king, shows up in their answer. They point to the silver they found in the mouths of their sacks and brought back from Canaan. Then they ask why they'd steal silver or gold from his master's house. Nobody drags Pharaoh into this, which is probably smart.

The brothers offer that deal, but the steward doesn't take it. He says, "As you say," and then changes the terms. "…only the one who is found with the cup will be my slave, and the rest of you shall be free of blame." So the rest of them walk free.

Right, the steward trims the deal way down. The brothers said whoever has the cup dies and the rest become slaves. He answers, "As you say," then adds, "But only the one who is found with the cup will be my slave, and the rest of you shall be free of blame." That's a much lighter sentence than the one they offered themselves.

Oldest first. The steward searches, "beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest." That means Benjamin's sack is dead last, so the brothers sweat through every sack before it. It's a long line to stand in with your hands shaking.

The youngest is where the search ends, not where it starts. The steward goes "beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest." Benjamin is the youngest, so his sack is the very last one opened. He gets to watch all his brothers go first.

Nobody gets ranked by muscle here. The steward goes by age, "beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest." Strength doesn't count when you're standing next to a donkey waiting on a sack inspection.

Yes, they do. After the cup is found, they all tear their clothes, load their donkeys, and go back to the city. Tearing clothes shows how hard the news hit them. They had barely gotten started on the road home, and now they're turning around.
They do go back, all of them. The text says they tore their clothes, loaded their donkeys, and returned to the city. It also says it was "they all" doing it. Nobody takes the road home that day.

That's Judah's answer. He's one of the brothers, and he says, "God has exposed the iniquity of your servants." He doesn't argue or fight the charge. He just puts it plainly and says they are now Joseph's slaves.

explanations.answer: Sent the famine as a warning
explanations.explanation: Judah never mentions the famine here. He's standing in front of Joseph after the cup turned up, and his words are, "God has exposed the iniquity of your servants." He doesn't make excuses or point at anything else.

explanations.answer: Sent the steward to test them
explanations.explanation: Judah never says anything about a test. What he says is, "God has exposed the iniquity of your servants." The steward isn't mentioned in his words at all. He keeps his answer short and doesn't dodge.

explanations.answer: All the brothers along with Benjamin
explanations.explanation: Judah puts everyone in it. He says, "We are now my lord's slaves…" and he names "both we and the one who was found with the cup." That means the brothers and Benjamin together. It's a lot of loyalty to put in one sentence.

explanations.answer: Only the oldest of the brothers
explanations.explanation: Judah doesn't narrow it down to one brother. He says "We are now my lord's slaves…" and adds "both we and the one who was found with the cup." That covers all of them. Nobody gets to sit this one out.

Judah says the opposite, because he includes Benjamin right in the sentence. He says, "We are now my lord's slaves…" and adds "both we and the one who was found with the cup." Benjamin is the one with the cup in his sack. Judah isn't leaving him to face it alone.

Dead is what they told Joseph. They said, "The boy's brother is dead." That's their story, and Joseph is standing right in front of them while they say it. They have no clue who they're talking to. I think that one had to land hard in the room.
Nobody says blind. The brothers told Joseph, "The boy's brother is dead." That's why their father holds so tightly to the boy who's left. Blindness doesn't come up in what Judah says.

Sick isn't the word. Judah says they told Joseph, "The boy's brother is dead." This is a heavy part of the story, so I'll just say plainly that it's a hard thing to say out loud. They didn't say anything about illness.

They did say that. They told Joseph, "The boy cannot leave his father. If he were to leave, his father would die." So Joseph knew the risk long before the cup ever turned up. Judah is reminding him of every word.

They did warn him, so this one is true. Judah says they told Joseph, "The boy cannot leave his father. If he were to leave, his father would die." Joseph had been told the cost before anything else happened. Judah is walking him back through it.

They said the opposite. They told their father, "We cannot go down there unless our younger brother goes with us." They add that if he isn't with them, they cannot see the man. So Benjamin was the ticket back in.

That's right, they pushed back. They told their father, "We cannot go down there unless our younger brother goes with us." And then, "So if our younger brother is not with us, we cannot see the man." No Benjamin, no meeting.

That's what Jacob said. He's the father of these brothers, and he told them, "Surely he has been torn to pieces." He adds that he hasn't seen that son since. I think this one hurts, and Jacob is still carrying it.

explanations.answer: He'd been lost in the desert
explanations.explanation: That's not what Jacob said. His words were, "Surely he has been torn to pieces." He says he has not seen that son since. This is a painful part of the story, so I'll just say he is describing a deep loss.
No river in Jacob's words. He said, "Surely he has been torn to pieces." Judah is quoting him word for word to Joseph. This is a sad moment, and I think it's meant to be heard slowly.

explanations.answer: Send him to his grave in sorrow
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jacob says that if they take Benjamin and harm comes to him, "you will bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow." Sheol is the grave, the place of the dead. He's telling them how heavy a second loss would be.

explanations.answer: Make him leave Canaan for good
explanations.explanation: Moving away isn't in Jacob's words. He says that if harm comes to Benjamin, "you will bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow." Sheol means the grave. He's talking about sorrow that would put him in the ground.

explanations.answer: Turn him against all of his sons
explanations.explanation: Jacob never says he'd turn on his sons. He says, "you will bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow." Sheol is the grave. I think he's showing how much it would break him, not how angry he'd be.

That's it. Judah says, "your servant guaranteed the boy's safety to my father." He told his father he would bear the guilt all his life if he didn't bring the boy back. So when he asks to stay, he's keeping his word.

explanations.answer: He paid for the grain himself
explanations.explanation: Judah never says he paid for the grain. What he tells Joseph is that he guaranteed the boy's safety to their father. He said he would bear the guilt all his life if he didn't bring him back. The promise cost more than any grain.

explanations.answer: He promised to bring more grain
explanations.explanation: Grain isn't what Judah promised. He says, "your servant guaranteed the boy's safety to my father." Their father wanted food, but Judah's promise was about Benjamin coming home. That's the one he's trying to keep.

explanations.answer: Keep Judah as a slave in place of the boy
explanations.explanation: That's the big ask. Judah says, "Now please let your servant stay here as my lord's slave in place of the boy. Let him return with his brothers." He offers himself so Benjamin can go home. That's a real turn from the brother who once said to sell Joseph.

explanations.answer: Let the brothers buy the boy back later
explanations.explanation: No buy-back plan comes up. Judah asks, "Now please let your servant stay here as my lord's slave in place of the boy." He wants the boy to go back with his brothers. He offers himself, not a deal.

explanations.answer: Take double the silver in place of the boy
explanations.explanation: Judah doesn't offer money at all. He begs, "Now please let your servant stay here as my lord's slave in place of the boy." What he's putting on the table is himself. Silver doesn't come into his plea.

Misery is the word. Judah says, "I could not bear to see the misery that would overwhelm him." He's picturing his father's face when Benjamin isn't there. That's why he's asking Joseph to take him instead.

Anger isn't what Judah is afraid of. He says, "I could not bear to see the misery that would overwhelm him." He's thinking about how his father would hurt, not how he'd yell. It's a sadder picture than that.
Shame isn't the word Judah uses. He says, "I could not bear to see the misery that would overwhelm him." It's all about what his father would go through. Judah's own feelings come second.
